newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korean news agency debuts on Internet.
newsitem.headline: North Korean news agency debuts on Internet.

text.p: North Korea formally made its debut on the Internet on Thursday in what one of its officials said was a bid to remove "misunderstandings" about one of the world's most reclusive nations.
Reports in English from the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) were made available to Internet users worldwide.
In the first stages of the project, KCNA reports will go on the Internet one day later than they are issued in their present traditional news agency form.

An official from the Korea News Service (KNS), which acts as the Japanese agent for the Pyongyang news agency, said North Korea also planned eventually to disseminate information on the World Wide Web in the Korean and Japanese languages.

"As is well-known, for a number of reasons, information about the DPRK (North Korea) has not been correctly conveyed to the outside world," Son Jin-Hyong, president of the Korea News Service, told Reuters Television.
"As a result, there are a lot of misunderstandings and distorted information about the DPRK. The aim of the home page is to see that information about the DPRK is correctly disseminated," he said.

KCNA, which marked the 50th anniversary of its founding last month, is regarded as the official voice of North Korea and the communist nation often makes important announcements through the news agency.
Son said North Korea, which has suffered famine after two consecutive years of flooding, saw the need to tell the world the truth through the Internet.
"Two years ago -- and again last year -- the country suffered heavy flood damage. As a result, there is in fact a shortage of food," he said.
"As a result we recognised a need to relay information about the floods to the world through the Internet," he said.
In a KCNA report to mark the debut, which did not appear on the Internet home page, North Korea bitterly accused rival South Korea of trying to deny its people access to the North Korean home page.
"The (South Korean President) Kim Young-sam group talk about 'danger' and 'side effects' of the 'home page'," North Korea's official daily Rodong Sinmun said.

"In view of national reconciliation and reunification, it should be regarded as fortunate that the South Korean students and people can see, through the Internet, and admire the realities of the Northern half of Korea where the great Juche (self-reliance) idea is carried into practice," it said.
Last month, authorities in South Korea warned Internet providers there that they risked lengthy jail terms if they distributed Pyongyang information.

South Korea blocked access to a Canadian-based Internet service provider last year after a Canadian student opened a page carrying North Korean information. It lifted the restriction after the page was closed.
South Korea bans the distribution of any information or material regarded as benefiting North Korea and violators can be jailed for up to seven years.
North and South Korea have remained technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended with a truce.
